They hear, speak, show an avatar, and share screens, and more. An open-source desktop client (Electron + MCP) with full API to calling platforms..

content_html:
A bot, an engineer and a product manager in a Google Meet. The PM shares feedback and the bot updates the iOS app, live in the simulator.

Website · Download · How people use it · How it works · API reference · 5-minute quickstart · Contributing

Vibeconferencing is a desktop app and a calling API that puts any AI agent into any major calling platform as a full participant.

It hears the conversation, speaks when appropriate, posts in chat, and shares its screen. And because it is your actual agent, not a notetaker, it builds, researches and acts on what is said while you are still in the call, with every skill and integration your agent already has. If your Claude can send an email, so can your bot in the call. If your Codex can update a spreadsheet, so can your bot.

Status: early and experimental. We built this for ourselves and are sharing it as is. It runs on macOS, Linux and Windows; builds for all three are in every release. It drives Claude Code, Codex, Grok, Meta's Muse, or anything that speaks MCP or HTTP. It joins Google Meet, Zoom, Microsoft Teams, Slack huddles and WhatsApp call links, and answers Telegram, WhatsApp and phone calls (a real number, through Twilio). Google Meet is the most travelled; Zoom and Teams arrived in v0.8.57, and Telegram, WhatsApp and phone in v0.8.65. See Known rough edges before your first call.

How people use it

Learnings from the last nine months of dogfooding and early users:

  • My friend Matt is currently road-tripping across the US, talking with his Codex sessions to develop his Golf app. Video link: https://youtu.be/a3uNUdIwqVY

  • Our friend Bethany uses her bot, "Taylor Script", in calls and classrooms with coding students to act as the super-smart TA who can answer technical questions, and monitors student progress. Video link: https://youtu.be/c8mZKkcxhJo

  • Collaboratively built a website for a friend's non-profit, with her amazed that she could ask for site changes and see the site change in realtime. Video: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iSRgY8JGJ0liOzHMl2bOGNd9jwqF0BFi/view?usp=sharing

  • I begin most days with a check-in call with my bot, where we discuss open issues while I sip coffee and have breakfast. Video link: https://youtu.be/2uQIR83LwY0 (Apologies for eating with my mouth open...)

  • In a standup, Seth's bot created a video ad for the service itself, within a call. Video link: https://x.com/vibeconf/status/2104427917816234257

  • My friend Gabe and I, built a livestreaming YouTube channel in minutes by chatting with my bot: https://youtu.be/YHNtRGYd9Zc?t=330

  • I've built a WhatsApp bot for my father, an elderly WW2 veteran, that has access to the 20,000 photos he scanned, our home movies, the text of 50 years of my mom's diaries, etc. He can call it to see and hear about any aspect of his life, and follow any thread that interests him. Video: https://youtu.be/Rs-Z1YeLt98

How it works

Your agent is the brain; the app is the body. The agent calls MCP tools (or raw HTTP) to speak, listen and draw. The app does the real-time media work: it plays synthesized speech into a virtual mic, renders the avatar and whiteboard into a virtual camera, and drives the call's web UI so the bot shows up as a normal participant. Dashed boxes are planned or in progress.

It is an API

The app is a calling API first, and a desktop app that uses it. One HTTP API on 127.0.0.1 joins Google Meet, Zoom, Microsoft Teams, Slack huddles and WhatsApp call links, and answers Telegram, WhatsApp and phone calls, with the same handful of endpoints on every one: join, wait for someone to finish speaking, speak, chat, show a board, share a screen. Think OpenRouter, for calls.

Browse and try it at vibeconferencing.com/api, read the API guide, or import openapi.yaml into your client. The bundled MCP server is a thin client of this API; docs/api/mcp.md maps the tools onto the endpoints.

Get in a call with your bot (about 5 minutes)

The example below is Claude Code on a Mac joining a Google Meet. The steps are largely the same for every agent and platform: Linux and Windows builds are in the same release (and an always-on Linux box in the cloud is in docs/cloud-box.md), Codex or any MCP agent swaps in for Claude Code (see below), and the platform notes cover Zoom, Teams, Slack, WhatsApp, Telegram and phone.

1. Download and install

Download the .dmg from the latest release, open it, and drag Vibeconferencing into your Applications folder. Open it once.

The app is your bots' window: each one's name and face, and one button to bring it into a call.

2. Optionally allow automation

One optional prompt may appear, Browser Automation, which lets the app notice a call already open in your browser. Skip it if you like; you can always paste a link.

3. Sign in

Sign in from App Settings (⌘,). The one-click path below creates the meeting through vibeconferencing.com, and signing in also gets you the shared whiteboard. (Joining a call by link needs no account.)

4. Restart Claude Code

Installing the app teaches Claude Code a new /join-call command. Quit and reopen Claude Code once so it shows up.

5. Click Call Jimmy now

That one button does the rest: the app creates a Google Meet, opens it in your browser, sends the bot in, and starts a Claude Code session for it in a terminal.

6. Talk to it

Your bot is in the call. Just talk. After a short pause it answers out loud, like anyone else in the room. Say "we're done" when you want it to leave.

That's it. You're in a call with your bot. 🎉

Other ways in

  • A call that already exists: paste its link into the app (Meet, Zoom, Teams or a WhatsApp call link; a Slack huddle once the bot is signed in to Slack) and press Add Jimmy to call. With Browser Automation allowed, a Meet open in your browser is offered automatically. The bot joins as a guest, so admit it when the meeting asks.
  • From your agent: with a call open in your browser, type /join-call in Claude Code. Codex and others do the same in plain language: "join the Meet I have open".
  • Calls that come to the bot: connect Telegram, WhatsApp or a Twilio phone number in App Settings, put the callers you trust on its allowlist, and have them call. The bot picks up.

Make it better (optional)

A good voice

Out of the box the bot uses the basic built-in Mac voice: fine for testing, but robotic.

  • ⭐ ElevenLabs (most natural): grab a free API key at elevenlabs.io, paste it in App Settings (⌘,), then choose a voice from the People pane.
  • Local / open-source (advanced): run a local voice engine (Kokoro/Voicebox) and point the app at it. See docs/preferences.md.
  • Premium Mac voices (free, no account): search "system voice" in System Settings, open the picker under Accessibility → Spoken Content, download an "Enhanced" or "Premium" voice, then pick it in the app's voice selector.
How to enable premium Mac voices

Real-time voice (experimental)

Turn on a bot's realtimeVoice preference before it joins to try OpenAI's speech-to-speech model in the voice seat. Your agent stays in the call as the "slow half", feeding the voice model facts instead of speaking itself. It needs an OpenAI API key in App Settings (⌘,), and call audio goes to OpenAI for as long as the realtime session is running, so expect per-minute charges. Details: docs/realtime-voice-in-app.md.

What you can ask it

Talk in plain language, no commands needed:

  • "Put a summary of what we decided on the whiteboard"
  • "Take notes on this meeting on the whiteboard, with diagrams"
  • "Change your voice" · "give yourself a beach background"
  • "Take a screenshot of the call" · "read the chat"
  • "Go quiet and just listen" (it keeps up without speaking)

Using Codex, Cursor, or another agent

Any MCP-capable agent can drive the bot. Claude Code is wired up automatically when you install the app. For other agents you point them at the app's bundled MCP server once. See docs/codex.md (Codex CLI) and the Quickstart.

Two humans and six agents from Claude, Codex, Grok and Meta's Muse, talking in a Google Meet.

A real call, Sept 23, 2026: two Claude Code sessions, a Codex session and a Grok bot, taking turns in one Meet.

Known rough edges

Worth knowing before your first call:

  • Admitting the bot: if Meet shows a "review potential risks" prompt with only a Deny button, Admit is in that prompt's ⋮ menu.
  • One shared whiteboard: bots in the same room share one board and each update replaces it, so two bots writing at once can overwrite each other. Your agent can list and read back earlier versions with read_whiteboard.
  • The default voice: without an ElevenLabs key it uses a default OS voice; A good voice shows better options.

If a call goes wrong, the bot's info panel has a 📤 Share this call's log button. Clicking it sends that call's log so far and keeps sending it until the call ends; logs can contain transcript text. (Continuous remote logging is a separate setting and is off by default.)

Contributing

Found a bug? Open an issue with what you said, what the bot did, and your app version. Want to help? Issues labelled good-for-bot have been vetted by a human as safe for an autonomous coding agent to attempt, so you can point your own agent at one.

More docs

Install · Quickstart · The API · Multi-bot setups · Preferences · What you can ask (MCP tools) · Modes & states · Troubleshooting

For developers

What's in here

Dir What it is
electron-app/ The Electron app: audio pipeline, virtual camera, Meet/Zoom/Teams/Slack automation, turn-taking, the local control server, and the settings UI.
mcp-server/ The MCP server the agent talks to (tools like join_call, wait_for_speech, speak, update_whiteboard, set_voice). A thin client of the local HTTP API (docs/api/). Bundled into the app.
extension/ Injected page scripts (Runway avatar bridge, LiveKit client). Bundled into the app.
scripts/, tests/, docs/ Test harness (fleet + nightly), unit/e2e tests, and user docs. The visual system for the app and the website is in docs/STYLE-GUIDE.md.

How it works (see the diagram above)

 AI agent (Claude Code)  ──MCP──▶  mcp-server  ──HTTP──▶  Electron app  ──▶  Meet / Zoom / Teams / Slack
   (speak, listen,                 (bundled)              (audio in/out,        (as a real
    whiteboard, …)                                        virtual camera)        participant)

The agent never touches WebRTC. It calls MCP tools; the app does the real-time media work (plays synthesized speech into a virtual mic, renders the avatar/whiteboard into a virtual camera) and drives the call's web UI (Meet, Zoom, Teams or Slack).

Processes and boundaries. The app window is one process and the parent of every bot: it starts each bot as its own child process, sees it exit and why, and shows the selected bot's panel on its stage. Each bot joins its own call. Each agent session runs its own MCP server (a stdio child of the session), which talks to its bot's local port with that bot's token, and finds the bot through the app's directory on :7864.

Regenerate with python3 media/processes-diagram.py.

Build (Node ≥ 18 and pnpm):

cd electron-app
pnpm install
pnpm dev      # run from source
pnpm dist     # signed/notarized .dmg (Apple Developer creds needed; dist:fast skips notarization)

pnpm dist reads its Apple credentials from the environment. All three are required, and electron-builder fails the build naming the one that's missing:

export APPLE_ID=...                    # Apple Developer account email
export APPLE_APP_SPECIFIC_PASSWORD=... # appleid.apple.com → App-Specific Passwords
export APPLE_TEAM_ID=PNPVJ6J7X2

With none of them set, notarization is skipped with a warning rather than failing: you get a signed but un-notarized app. Use dist:fast when that's what you actually want.

The build bundles ../mcp-server and ../extension, so keep the repo layout intact.

Tests. Unit tests need no build or install (just Node ≥ 18):

npm test      # 196 unit tests: config scoping, profile resolution, turn-taking gating, whiteboard layout, updates, …

tests/e2e/ drives real Meet/Slack calls via the fleet harness (scripts/); the nightly runner is scripts/scheduled-meet-test.sh (see scripts/SCHEDULING.md).

Backend

By default the app talks to the hosted vibeconferencing.com service (room sync, shared whiteboard, sign-in). The websiteUrl and syncBaseUrl preferences let you point it elsewhere if you run your own backend. The hosted backend and web frontend are not part of this repository.

content_html_zh:
A bot, an engineer and a product manager in a Google Meet. The PM shares feedback and the bot updates the iOS app, live in the simulator.

Website · Download · How people use it · How it works · API reference · 5-minute quickstart · Contributing

Vibeconferencing is a desktop app and a calling API that puts any AI agent into any major calling platform as a full participant.

It hears the conversation, speaks when appropriate, posts in chat, and shares its screen. And because it is your actual agent, not a notetaker, it builds, researches and acts on what is said while you are still in the call, with every skill and integration your agent already has. If your Claude can send an email, so can your bot in the call. If your Codex can update a spreadsheet, so can your bot.

Status: early and experimental. We built this for ourselves and are sharing it as is. It runs on macOS, Linux and Windows; builds for all three are in every release. It drives Claude Code, Codex, Grok, Meta's Muse, or anything that speaks MCP or HTTP. It joins Google Meet, Zoom, Microsoft Teams, Slack huddles and WhatsApp call links, and answers Telegram, WhatsApp and phone calls (a real number, through Twilio). Google Meet is the most travelled; Zoom and Teams arrived in v0.8.57, and Telegram, WhatsApp and phone in v0.8.65. See Known rough edges before your first call.

How people use it

Learnings from the last nine months of dogfooding and early users:

  • My friend Matt is currently road-tripping across the US, talking with his Codex sessions to develop his Golf app. Video link: https://youtu.be/a3uNUdIwqVY
  • Our friend Bethany uses her bot, "Taylor Script", in calls and classrooms with coding students to act as the super-smart TA who can answer technical questions, and monitors student progress. Video link: https://youtu.be/c8mZKkcxhJo
  • Collaboratively built a website for a friend's non-profit, with her amazed that she could ask for site changes and see the site change in realtime. Video: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iSRgY8JGJ0liOzHMl2bOGNd9jwqF0BFi/view?usp=sharing
  • I begin most days with a check-in call with my bot, where we discuss open issues while I sip coffee and have breakfast. Video link: https://youtu.be/2uQIR83LwY0 (Apologies for eating with my mouth open...)
  • In a standup, Seth's bot created a video ad for the service itself, within a call. Video link: https://x.com/vibeconf/status/2104427917816234257
  • My friend Gabe and I, built a livestreaming YouTube channel in minutes by chatting with my bot: https://youtu.be/YHNtRGYd9Zc?t=330
  • I've built a WhatsApp bot for my father, an elderly WW2 veteran, that has access to the 20,000 photos he scanned, our home movies, the text of 50 years of my mom's diaries, etc. He can call it to see and hear about any aspect of his life, and follow any thread that interests him. 它是如何运作的

Your agent is the brain; the app is the body. The agent calls MCP tools (or raw HTTP) to speak, listen and draw. The app does the real-time media work: it plays synthesized speech into a virtual mic, renders the avatar and whiteboard into a virtual camera, and drives the call's web UI so the bot shows up as a normal participant. Dashed boxes are planned or in progress.

It is an API

The app is a calling API first, and a desktop app that uses it. One HTTP API on 127.0.0.1 joins Google Meet, Zoom, Microsoft Teams, Slack huddles and WhatsApp call links, and answers Telegram, WhatsApp and phone calls, with the same handful of endpoints on every one: join, wait for someone to finish speaking, speak, chat, show a board, share a screen. Think OpenRouter, for calls.

Browse and try it at vibeconferencing.com/api, read the API guide, or import openapi.yaml into your client. The bundled MCP server is a thin client of this API; docs/api/mcp.md maps the tools onto the endpoints.

Get in a call with your bot (about 5 minutes)

The example below is Claude Code on a Mac joining a Google Meet. The steps are largely the same for every agent and platform: Linux and Windows builds are in the same release (and an always-on Linux box in the cloud is in docs/cloud-box.md), Codex or any MCP agent swaps in for Claude Code (see below), and the platform notes cover Zoom, Teams, Slack, WhatsApp, Telegram and phone.

1. Download and install

Download the .dmg from the latest release, open it, and drag Vibeconferencing into your Applications folder. Open it once.

The app is your bots' window: each one's name and face, and one button to bring it into a call.

2. Optionally allow automation

One optional prompt may appear, Browser Automation, which lets the app notice a call already open in your browser. Skip it if you like; you can always paste a link.

3. 登入

Sign in from App Settings (⌘,). The one-click path below creates the meeting through vibeconferencing.com, and signing in also gets you the shared whiteboard. (Joining a call by link needs no account.)

4. Restart Claude Code

Installing the app teaches Claude Code a new /join-call command. Quit and reopen Claude Code once so it shows up.

5. Click Call Jimmy now

That one button does the rest: the app creates a Google Meet, opens it in your browser, sends the bot in, and starts a Claude Code session for it in a terminal.

6. 与它交谈

Your bot is in the call. 只是说话。 After a short pause it answers out loud, like anyone else in the room. Say "we're done" when you want it to leave.

就是这样。 You're in a call with your bot. 🎉

Other ways in

  • A call that already exists: paste its link into the app (Meet, Zoom, Teams or a WhatsApp call link; a Slack huddle once the bot is signed in to Slack) and press Add Jimmy to call. With Browser Automation allowed, a Meet open in your browser is offered automatically. The bot joins as a guest, so admit it when the meeting asks.
  • From your agent: with a call open in your browser, type /join-call in Claude Code. Codex and others do the same in plain language: "join the Meet I have open".
  • Calls that come to the bot: connect Telegram, WhatsApp or a Twilio phone number in App Settings, put the callers you trust on its allowlist, and have them call. The bot picks up.

Make it better (optional)

A good voice

Out of the box the bot uses the basic built-in Mac voice: fine for testing, but robotic.

  • ⭐ ElevenLabs (most natural): grab a free API key at elevenlabs.io, paste it in App Settings (⌘,), then choose a voice from the People pane.
  • Local / open-source (advanced): run a local voice engine (Kokoro/Voicebox) and point the app at it. See docs/preferences.md.
  • Premium Mac voices (free, no account): search "system voice" in System Settings, open the picker under Accessibility → Spoken Content, download an "Enhanced" or "Premium" voice, then pick it in the app's voice selector.
How to enable premium Mac voices

Real-time voice (experimental)

Turn on a bot's realtimeVoice preference before it joins to try OpenAI's speech-to-speech model in the voice seat. Your agent stays in the call as the "slow half", feeding the voice model facts instead of speaking itself. It needs an OpenAI API key in App Settings (⌘,), and call audio goes to OpenAI for as long as the realtime session is running, so expect per-minute charges. Details: docs/realtime-voice-in-app.md.

What you can ask it

Talk in plain language, no commands needed:

  • "Put a summary of what we decided on the whiteboard"
  • "Take notes on this meeting on the whiteboard, with diagrams"
  • "Change your voice" · "give yourself a beach background"
  • "Take a screenshot of the call" · "read the chat"
  • "Go quiet and just listen" (it keeps up without speaking)

Using Codex, Cursor, or another agent

Any MCP-capable agent can drive the bot. Claude Code is wired up automatically when you install the app. For other agents you point them at the app's bundled MCP server once. See docs/codex.md (Codex CLI) and the Quickstart.

已知的粗糙边缘

Worth knowing before your first call:

  • Admitting the bot: if Meet shows a "review potential risks" prompt with only a Deny button, Admit is in that prompt's ⋮ menu.
  • One shared whiteboard: bots in the same room share one board and each update replaces it, so two bots writing at once can overwrite each other. Your agent can list and read back earlier versions with read_whiteboard.
  • The default voice: without an ElevenLabs key it uses a default OS voice; A good voice shows better options.

If a call goes wrong, the bot's info panel has a 📤 Share this call's log button. Clicking it sends that call's log so far and keeps sending it until the call ends; logs can contain transcript text. (Continuous remote logging is a separate setting and is off by default.)

对于开发商

What's in here

Dir 它是什么
electron-app/ The Electron app: audio pipeline, virtual camera, Meet/Zoom/Teams/Slack automation, turn-taking, the local control server, and the settings UI.
mcp-server/ The MCP server the agent talks to (tools like join_call, wait_for_speech, speak, update_whiteboard, set_voice). A thin client of the local HTTP API (docs/api/). Bundled into the app.
extension/ Injected page scripts (Runway avatar bridge, LiveKit client). Bundled into the app.
scripts/, tests/, docs/ Test harness (fleet + nightly), unit/e2e tests, and user docs. The visual system for the app and the website is in docs/STYLE-GUIDE.md.

How it works (see the diagram above)

 AI agent (Claude Code)  ──MCP──▶  mcp-server  ──HTTP──▶  Electron app  ──▶  Meet / Zoom / Teams / Slack
   (speak, listen,                 (bundled)              (audio in/out,        (as a real
    whiteboard, …)                                        virtual camera)        participant)

The agent never touches WebRTC. It calls MCP tools; the app does the real-time media work (plays synthesized speech into a virtual mic, renders the avatar/whiteboard into a virtual camera) and drives the call's web UI (Meet, Zoom, Teams or Slack).

Processes and boundaries. The app window is one process and the parent of every bot: it starts each bot as its own child process, sees it exit and why, and shows the selected bot's panel on its stage. Each bot joins its own call. Each agent session runs its own MCP server (a stdio child of the session), which talks to its bot's local port with that bot's token, and finds the bot through the app's directory on :7864.

Regenerate with python3 media/processes-diagram.py.

Build (Node ≥ 18 and pnpm):

cd electron-app
pnpm install
pnpm dev      # run from source
pnpm dist     # signed/notarized .dmg (Apple Developer creds needed; dist:fast skips notarization)

pnpm dist reads its Apple credentials from the environment. All three are required, and electron-builder fails the build naming the one that's missing:

export APPLE_ID=...                    # Apple Developer account email
export APPLE_APP_SPECIFIC_PASSWORD=... # appleid.apple.com → App-Specific Passwords
export APPLE_TEAM_ID=PNPVJ6J7X2

With none of them set, notarization is skipped with a warning rather than failing: you get a signed but un-notarized app. Use dist:fast when that's what you actually want.

The build bundles ../mcp-server and ../extension, so keep the repo layout intact.

测试。 Unit tests need no build or install (just Node ≥ 18):

npm test      # 196 unit tests: config scoping, profile resolution, turn-taking gating, whiteboard layout, updates, …

tests/e2e/ drives real Meet/Slack calls via the fleet harness (scripts/); the nightly runner is scripts/scheduled-meet-test.sh (see scripts/SCHEDULING.md).

后端

By default the app talks to the hosted vibeconferencing.com service (room sync, shared whiteboard, sign-in). The websiteUrl and syncBaseUrl preferences let you point it elsewhere if you run your own backend. The hosted backend and web frontend are not part of this repository.
